question: What is the main difference between a wound dressing and a bandage?

options.A: A dressing is only for bone fractures, and bandages are for skin cuts.
options.B: A bandage absorbs drainage, while a dressing provides structural support.
options.C: A bandage is always sterile, whereas dressings are never sterile.
options.D: A dressing touches the wound directly, while a bandage holds the dressing in place.

explanation: Think of it this way: the dressing is the sweet layer right on the open skin soaking up fluids, while the bandage wraps around it to keep everything secure. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h1)

question: Why do modern nurses prefer keeping a wound environment moist?

options.A: It leaves the wound completely open to fresh air safely.
options.B: It keeps the body from producing any fluid at all.
options.C: It stops all bacterial growth on the skin completely.
options.D: It lets skin cells repair faster and helps prevent harsh scarring.

explanation: Skin cells love moisture! They glide across a moist wound bed way faster than trying to crawl across a dry, crusty scab. Great nursing knowledge to keep in your pocket. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h1)

question: Which type of wound is created under clean, controlled hospital conditions?
explanation: An intentional wound is just a planned surgical cut made by a surgeon using strict sterile steps. Nice and straightforward! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h2)

question: How do partial-thickness and full-thickness wounds differ in how they heal?

options.A: Partial-thickness wounds heal by skin cell regeneration, while full-thickness wounds need granulation tissue and a scar.
options.B: Full-thickness wounds never form scar tissue like shallow cuts do.
options.C: Partial-thickness wounds go all the way into the muscle layer.
options.D: Partial-thickness wounds always need skin grafts, but full-thickness ones heal on their own.

explanation: When a wound goes deep (full-thickness), the body has to build new tissue from the bottom up to fill the gap before it can close. You're learning clinical anatomy like a pro! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h2)

question: Which dressing material comes from seaweed and turns into a soft gel when it meets heavy wound fluid?
explanation: Alginates are made from seaweed and are superstars at soaking up heavy drainage while forming a comfy gel. Pretty cool nursing trivia! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h3)

question: A patient has a deep pressure ulcer on their heel that is draining a lot of fluid. Which dressing is best to handle it?
explanation: Foam dressings are fantastic at cushioning fragile skin while soaking up moderate-to-heavy drainage. Spot on! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h3)

question: What do we call wound drainage that is clear and watery?
explanation: Serous fluid comes from plasma—think of the clear liquid you see in a minor blister. Easy terminology to lock down! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h4)

question: When should you usually give a patient their pain medication before a scheduled dressing change?

options.A: Right after you finish the dressing change
options.C: Only if the patient starts crying
options.D: Two hours before so it wears off

explanation: Giving pain meds about half an hour early gives the drug time to kick in right when you start cleaning sensitive tissue. Patient comfort is key! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h4)

question: When you are cleaning a wound, what is the safest direction to wipe?

options.A: From the outer edges inward to the center
options.B: From the cleanest area to the dirtiest area
options.C: In a wild circular motion all over the skin
options.D: From the bottom of the wound straight up

explanation: Always move from clean to dirty! This golden rule stops you from dragging germs from the surrounding skin right back into the open wound. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h5)

question: What must you do if an unsterile object accidentally touches your sterile field while setting up?

options.A: Throw away the whole field and set up a fresh sterile kit.
options.B: Spray antiseptic over the area and wait two minutes.
options.C: Wipe the spot with alcohol and keep going.
options.D: Ignore it if the object looked clean enough.

explanation: Safety first! If a sterile field is touched by something unsterile, its clean status is broken and you have to start fresh. Better safe than sorry in infection control. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h5)

question: What should you do if an old gauze dressing is stuck tightly to a healing wound?

options.A: Leave the old gauze stuck and put new dressings on top.
options.B: Moisten it gently with sterile normal saline to loosen it.
options.C: Soak the whole patient in hot soapy water.
options.D: Rip it off quickly with a fast jerk to save time.

explanation: Never rip dry gauze off! A little sterile saline softens the dried fluid and protects that precious new skin underneath. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h6)

question: Right after finishing a sterile dressing change, what final detail should you write on the dressing tape?

options.B: The date, time, and your initials.
options.C: The patient's diagnosis and room number.
options.D: A friendly smiley face for the patient.

explanation: Labeling your work lets the rest of the healthcare team know exactly when the dressing was changed and who did it. Professional habit unlocked! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h6)

question: Which of these details do you need to write in your nursing notes after a dressing change?

options.A: Wound size, color, and how much drainage you saw
options.B: The exact financial cost of the gauze packs
options.C: What the patient's family members think about it
options.D: The brand name of soap the patient uses at home

explanation: Documentation must stay clinical and objective so everyone can track whether the wound is actually getting better. You're thinking like a registered nurse! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h7)

question: What does healthy pink or red granulation tissue tell you about a wound?

options.A: A severe bacterial infection has taken over the site.
options.B: The wound is healing nicely with new blood vessel growth.
options.C: The tissue is dying and needs immediate surgery.
options.D: The dressing material is causing an allergic reaction.

explanation: Granulation tissue is packed with tiny new blood vessels. Seeing that healthy pink/red color is a huge nursing win! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h7)

question: What is the term for a surgical emergency where internal organs pop out through an opened surgical wound?
explanation: Evisceration is a scary medical emergency where organs protrude past the incision line. It needs immediate sterile coverage and a surgeon right away! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h8)

question: What is your very first nursing action if an abdominal wound suddenly pops open and organs are exposed?

options.A: Cover the organs with sterile saline-soaked dressings and call the surgeon.
options.B: Use your gloved fingers to push the organs back inside.
options.C: Wrap a tight binder around the belly to squeeze the organs back in.
options.D: Leave the wound completely open to the fresh air.

explanation: Keep those exposed organs moist with sterile saline gauze so they don't dry out while you call for emergency surgical help. Emergency handled like a champ! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h8)
